Appendix A Short-Range Behaviour

In this section, we derive the short-range behaviors of Abelian anyons, which we make heavy use of throughout the manuscript. We first consider the short-range behavior for non-interacting (“free”) anyons, and we note that this has been discussed previously in Ref. [5]. The calculation is easiest to do in the anyon gauge, but we will translate the result to the fermion gauge at the end. We consider the Hamiltonian for two free anyons, and study the form of the wavefunction near coincidence.

Hfree=−12​∇12−12​∇22=−14​∇𝐑2−∇𝐫2,\displaystyle H_{\text{free}}=-\frac{1}{2}\nabla^{2}_{1}-\frac{1}{2}\nabla^{2}_{2}=-\frac{1}{4}\nabla^{2}_{{\bf R}}-\nabla^{2}_{{\bf r}}, (59)

where we have transformed the Hamiltonian into center of mass (𝐑{\bf R}) and relative (𝐫{\bf r}) coordinates. The center of mass component plays no role in this analysis, so we inspect

Hrel=−∇𝐫2=−[∂2∂r2+1r​∂∂r+1r2​∂2∂θ2].\displaystyle H_{\rm rel}=-\nabla^{2}_{{\bf r}}=-\left[\frac{\partial^{2}}{\partial r^{2}}+\frac{1}{r}\frac{\partial}{\partial r}+\frac{1}{r^{2}}\frac{\partial^{2}}{\partial\theta^{2}}\right]. (60)

As we are dealing with hard-core anyons, r=0r=0 is a regular singular point, where the wavefunction vanishes. Near r=0r=0, we can expand the anyonic wavefunction (in the relative sector) as

ψA​(𝐫)=fn​(r)​ei⁡(α+2​n)​θ,\displaystyle\psi_{A}({\bf r})=f_{n}(r)e^{i(\alpha+2n)\theta}, (61)
fn​(r)=rγn​∑m=0am​rm,\displaystyle f_{n}(r)=r^{\gamma_{n}}\sum_{m=0}a_{m}r^{m}, (62)

where γn⩾0\gamma_{n}\geqslant 0. The choice of the relative angular momentum set to α+2​n\alpha+2n, n∈ℤn\in\mathbb{Z}, corresponds to the anyon exchange condition. Without loss of generality, we will insist on a0≠0a_{0}\neq 0, corresponding to γn\gamma_{n} being the minimal non-trivial exponent in this channel. Inserting this ansatz into the Schrödinger equation, we obtain

−\displaystyle- ∑m=0(γn+m)​(γn+m−1)​am​rγn+m−2−∑m=0(γn+m)​am​rγn+m−2+∑m=0(α+2​n)2​am​rγn+m−2=Erel​∑m=0am​rγn+m.\displaystyle\sum_{m=0}(\gamma_{n}+m)(\gamma_{n}+m-1)a_{m}r^{\gamma_{n}+m-2}-\sum_{m=0}(\gamma_{n}+m)a_{m}r^{\gamma_{n}+m-2}+\sum_{m=0}(\alpha+2n)^{2}a_{m}r^{\gamma_{n}+m-2}=E_{\rm rel}\sum_{m=0}a_{m}r^{\gamma_{n}+m}. (63)

Matching the coefficients on both sides, we obtain

γn2=(α+2​n)2⟹γn=|α+2​n|,\displaystyle\gamma_{n}^{2}=(\alpha+2n)^{2}\implies\gamma_{n}=|\alpha+2n|, (64)

where we have rejected the negative γ\gamma solutions based on our choice to focus on hardcore anyons. From this, we conclude that the allowed short-distance behaviors for ψA​(r)\psi_{A}(r) are

ψA∼r|α+2​n|​ei⁡(α+2​n)​θ,(n∈ℤ)\psi_{A}\sim r^{|\alpha+2n|}e^{i(\alpha+2n)\theta},\;\;(n\in\mathbb{Z}) (65)

up to multiplication of a smooth function that can be easily represented by a neural network. Translating this result into the fermion gauge, using Eq. (3), we obtain

ψF∼r|α+2​n|​ei⁡(1+2​n)​θ,(n∈ℤ)\psi_{F}\sim r^{|\alpha+2n|}e^{i(1+2n)\theta},\;\;(n\in\mathbb{Z}) (66)

which is the short-distance behavior quoted in Eq. (32).

Next, we consider how the Coulomb interaction between anyons modify the short-distance behaviors, which is incorporated into the AnyNet for studying the interacting anyonic atom in Sec. V. To that end, the relative sector HrelH_{\rm rel} contains an extra 1/r1/r term (recall we adopt the Hartree units, see Eq. (21) in the main text), and repeating the above analysis by substituting the above expansion ansatz into the Schrödinger equation, upon matching coefficients we obtain

γn=|α+2​n|anda1=a02​γn+1.\gamma_{n}=\absolutevalue{\alpha+2n}\quad\text{and}\quad a_{1}=\frac{a_{0}}{2\gamma_{n}+1}. (67)

Hence, statistics still fixes the leading power in the same way, while the Coulomb interaction fixes the next coefficient. In the fermion gauge, the short-distance behavior of the Coulomb-interacting anyonic wavefunction thus takes the form

ψF∼r|α+2​n|​ei⁡(1+2​n)​θ​[1+r2​|α+2​n|+1].\psi_{F}\sim r^{|\alpha+2n|}e^{i(1+2n)\theta}\left[1+\frac{r}{2|\alpha+2n|+1}\right]. (68)

This is the kind of short-range behavior that we build into the AnyNet for studying the interacting anyonic atom. See also the discussion in the main text around Eq. (41).

Appendix B Non-Relativistic Conformal Symmetry of the Free Anyon Hamiltonian

In this section, we follow the first-quantized analysis of [134], which was originally applied to the Fermi gas at unitary, to expose the structure of the free anyon eigenstates as a consequence of a non-relativistic conformal symmetry.

To keep things self-contained, we restate our model here, and also make re-introduce the constants set to 11 in the main text, in order to keep units explicit. The Hamiltonian is

H=ℏ22​m​∑i=1N[−i​∇i+𝐚i]2+m​ω22​∑i=1N|𝐫i|2,H=\frac{\hbar^{2}}{2m}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\left[-i\nabla_{i}+\mathbf{a}_{i}\right]^{2}+\frac{m\omega^{2}}{2}\sum_{i=1}^{N}|\mathbf{r}_{i}|^{2}, (69)

where

𝐚i=(α−1)​∑j≠i𝐳^×(𝐫i−𝐫j)|𝐫i−𝐫j|2.\mathbf{a}_{i}=(\alpha-1)\sum_{j\neq i}\frac{\widehat{\mathbf{z}}\times(\mathbf{r}_{i}-\mathbf{r}_{j})}{|\mathbf{r}_{i}-\mathbf{r}_{j}|^{2}}. (70)

We define the operators

𝑹\displaystyle\bm{R} ≡(𝒓1,𝒓2,…,𝒓N),\displaystyle\equiv(\bm{r}_{1},\bm{r}_{2},\ldots,\bm{r}_{N})\,, (71)
R2\displaystyle R^{2} ≡∑i|ri|2,\displaystyle\equiv\sum_{i}\absolutevalue{r_i}^{2}\,,
D^\displaystyle\widehat{D} ≡𝑹⋅∂𝑹,\displaystyle\equiv\bm{R}\cdot\partial_{\bm{R}}\,,
L±\displaystyle L_{\pm} =±N±D^+Hℏ​ω−m​ω​R2/ℏ.\displaystyle=\pm N\pm\widehat{D}+\frac{H}{\hbar\omega}-m\omega R^{2}/\hbar\,.

One can verify

[H,L±]\displaystyle\commutator{H}{L_{\pm}} =±2​ℏ​ω​L±,\displaystyle=\pm 2\hbar\omega L_{\pm}\,, (72)
[L+,L−]\displaystyle\commutator{L_+}{L_-} =−4​Hℏ​ω.\displaystyle=-\frac{4H}{\hbar\omega}\,.

We define the Casimir operator

𝒞^\displaystyle\widehat{\mathcal{C}} ≡H2−12​(ℏ​ω)2​(L+​L−+L−​L+)\displaystyle\equiv H^{2}-\frac{1}{2}(\hbar\omega)^{2}\left(L_{+}L_{-}+L_{-}L_{+}\right) (73)

which commutes with HH and L±L_{\pm}. For a ladder of energy eigenstates with constant 𝒞^\widehat{\mathcal{C}}, the Casimir takes the value C=Eg​(Eg−2​ℏ​ω)C=E_{g}(E_{g}-2\hbar\omega), where EgE_{g} is the energy of the lowest-energy state of the ladder (annihilated by L−L_{-}). This implies that EgE_{g} can be obtained by the operator

Hg≡ℏ​ω+𝒞^+(ℏ​ω)2.H_{g}\equiv\hbar\omega+\sqrt{\widehat{\mathcal{C}}+(\hbar\omega)^{2}}\,. (74)

We define the bosonic operators b,b†b\,,b^{\dagger} as

b\displaystyle b ≡ℏ​ω2​(H+Hg)​L−,\displaystyle\equiv\sqrt{\frac{\hbar\omega}{2(H+H_{g})}}L_{-}\,, (75)
b†\displaystyle b^{\dagger} ≡L+​ℏ​ω2​(H+Hg).\displaystyle\equiv L_{+}\sqrt{\frac{\hbar\omega}{2(H+H_{g})}}\,.

By introducing these operators, the Hamiltonian can be written exactly as

H=Hg+2​ℏ​ω​b†​b.H=H_{g}+2\hbar\omega b^{\dagger}b\,. (76)

So, the spectrum of the Hamiltonian splits into sectors with energies Eg,Eg+2​ℏ​ω,Eg+4​ℏ​ω​…E_{g}\,,E_{g}+2\hbar\omega\,,E_{g}+4\hbar\omega\ldots.

The lowest-energy state within a given tower, which includes the global ground state, obeys the equation L−​|ψ⟩=0L_{-}\ket{\psi}=0. Integrating this equation yields

ψ(𝑹)=e−R2/2a2REg/(ℏ​ω)−Nf(𝒏)\psi(\bm{R})=e^{-R^{2}/2a^{2}}R^{E_{g}/(\hbar\omega)-N}f(\bm{n}) (77)

where 𝒏≡𝑹/R\bm{n}\equiv\bm{R}/R is the unit vector, and a=ℏ/m​ωa=\sqrt{\hbar/m\omega} is the length scale of the harmonic oscillator . Hence, the ground state of an NN-anyon system can be written as a Gaussian envelope e−R2/2a2e^{-R^{2}/2a^{2}} times a homogenous function of degree Eg/(ℏ​ω)−NE_{g}/(\hbar\omega)-N.

This fixes the coalescence condition in the anyon wavefunction as MM anyons approach each other. For the ground state of NN anyons, the ground state wavefunction as all anyons approach each other must vanish as rEN/(ℏ​ω)−Nr^{E_{N}/(\hbar\omega)-N}, where ENE_{N} is the ground state energy of NN anyons. When M<NM<N anyons approach each other, the coalescence behavior is specified by the spectrum of the MM-anyon problem, with the leading-order exponent related to the MM-anyon ground state energy, EM/(ℏ​ω)−ME_{M}/(\hbar\omega)-M, although subleading exponents corresponding to excited states in the MM-anyon spectrum will also exist. The case of M=2M=2 particles corresponds to the analysis in App. A; the spectrum of the two anyon problem decomposes into two towers of energies, one with lowest energy ℏ​ω​(2+α)\hbar\omega(2+\alpha) and the other with lowest energy ℏ​ω​(4−α)\hbar\omega(4-\alpha). The two short-distance channels in our ansatz are necessary to capture both possibilities.

Appendix C Divergent Monte Carlo Variance

The many-body wavefunction must satisfy the short range behavior derived in Eq. (65) for every pair of particles. We show that failure to represent this short-range behavior results in a strong local energy (ELE_{L}) divergence, which causes the variance of the estimated energy expectation value to diverge.

We perform this calculation in the anyon gauge, and consider only the relative coordinates in complex representation, z≡(x1−x2)+i⁡(y1−y2)z\equiv(x_{1}-x_{2})+i(y_{1}-y_{2}). In this form, Hr=−4∂∂¯H_{r}=-4\partial\overline{\partial}, where ∂\partial (∂¯\overline{\partial}) is the holomorphic (antiholomorphic) derivative. As we are working in the anyon gauge, we require the phase be exp⁡[i​θ​(α+2​n)]\exp[i\theta(\alpha+2n)], with θ=arg⁡(z)\theta=\arg(z), n∈ℤn\in\mathbb{Z}, and allow for any radial power (we only consider the leading radial power). Such state can be generally written near coincidences as ψA​(z,z¯)=zγ+α+2​n​z¯γ\psi_{A}(z,\overline{z})=z^{\gamma+\alpha+2n}\overline{z}^{\gamma}.

EL\displaystyle E_{L} ∝z−(γ+α+2​n)​z¯−γ​∂z∂z¯zγ+α+2​n​z¯γ,\displaystyle\propto z^{-(\gamma+\alpha+2n)}\overline{z}^{-\gamma}\partial_{z}\partial_{\overline{z}}z^{\gamma+\alpha+2n}\overline{z}^{\gamma}, (78)
=(γ+α+2​n)​γz​z¯.\displaystyle=\frac{(\gamma+\alpha+2n)\gamma}{z\overline{z}}. (79)

The coefficient of the 1/r21/r^{2} vanishes if γ=0\gamma=0 (one of the channels in the positive branch) or γ+α+2​n=0\gamma+\alpha+2n=0 (one of the channels in the negative branch). Let Γ(=2​γ+α+2​n)\Gamma(=2\gamma+\alpha+2n), be the leading radial power of the state. Consider now the Monte Carlo variance (ignoring the finite term ⟨EL⟩2\langle E_{L}\rangle^{2}) due to random samples near coincidence of particles,

σ2\displaystyle\sigma^{2} ∼∫0R|ψ|2​(1r2)2​r​𝑑r,\displaystyle\sim\int_{0}^{R}|\psi|^{2}\left(\frac{1}{r^{2}}\right)^{2}rdr, (80)
∼∫0Rr2​Γ−3​𝑑r,\displaystyle\sim\int_{0}^{R}r^{2\Gamma-3}dr, (81)

which diverges near R=0R=0 unless Γ>1\Gamma>1. However, generic anyon wavefunctions have Γ≤1\Gamma\leq 1. Therefore, any ansatz with the correct radial power Γ\Gamma, will have a divergent Monte Carlo variance unless the short-range structure exactly matches the ones derived in Appendix A.

Appendix D Optimization

The network parameters were optimized to minimize the expectation value of the Hamiltonian.

⟨H⟩\displaystyle\langle H\rangle =∫d​𝑹​ψ¯​(𝑹)​H​ψ​(𝑹)∫d​𝑹​ψ¯​(𝑹)​ψ​(𝑹)=⟨EL​(𝑹)⟩𝑹∼|ψ⁡(𝑹)|2,\displaystyle=\frac{\int d\bm{R}\overline{\psi}(\bm{R})H\psi(\bm{R})}{\int d\bm{R}\overline{\psi}(\bm{R})\psi(\bm{R})}=\langle E_{L}(\bm{R})\rangle_{\bm{R}\sim|\psi(\bm{R})|^{2}}, (82)

where EL​(𝑹)=1ψ⁡(𝑹)​H​ψ​(𝑹)E_{L}(\bm{R})=\frac{1}{\psi(\bm{R})}H\psi(\bm{R}) is the local energy, and 𝑹\bm{R} is shortand for (𝒓1,…,𝒓N)(\bm{r}_{1},\dots,\bm{r}_{N}). The gradient with respect to variational parameters can be computed analytically as

∂θi⟨H⟩\displaystyle\partial_{\theta_{i}}\langle H\rangle =2​Re⁡[⟨EL​O¯i⟩−⟨EL⟩​⟨O¯i⟩],\displaystyle=2\operatorname{Re}[\langle E_{L}\overline{O}_{i}\rangle-\langle E_{L}\rangle\langle\overline{O}_{i}\rangle], (83)
Oi\displaystyle O_{i} =∂θilog⁡(ψ),\displaystyle=\partial_{\theta_{i}}\log(\psi), (84)

which is evaluated with Monte Carlo integration. The parameters were optimized with KFAC [80], details of the training and network hyperparameters used can be found in Table 3.

Appendix E Extrapolation of Exact Diagonalization Energies

In this appendix we describe the exact diagonalization used to obtain the N=4N=4 energies quoted in the main text. The construction follows [122], to which we refer the reader for the original derivation.

Starting with a wavefunction Ψ\Psi in the bosonic gauge, we perform a similarity transformation Ψ=∏i<j|ri−rj|α​Φ\Psi=\prod_{i<j}\absolutevalue{r_i - r_j}^{\alpha}\,\Phi. This similarity transformation removes the three-body interaction in the Hamiltonian, and the reduced Hamiltonian acting on Φ\Phi is non-Hermitian while retaining a real spectrum. For N=4N=4, we can use relative coordinates

x1\displaystyle x_{1} =12​(z1+z4−z2−z3),\displaystyle=\tfrac{1}{2}(z_{1}+z_{4}-z_{2}-z_{3})\,, (85)
x2\displaystyle x_{2} =12​(z2+z4−z1−z3),\displaystyle=\tfrac{1}{2}(z_{2}+z_{4}-z_{1}-z_{3})\,,
x3\displaystyle x_{3} =12​(z3+z4−z1−z2),\displaystyle=\tfrac{1}{2}(z_{3}+z_{4}-z_{1}-z_{2})\,,

which, together with X=12​(z1+z2+z3+z4)X=\tfrac{1}{2}(z_{1}+z_{2}+z_{3}+z_{4}), constitute an orthogonal change of variables. The oscillator part of the Hamiltonian is therefore unchanged and the physical center of mass XX separates exactly. Crucially, every pair separation is then a simple combination of two Moshinsky coordinates: one has z1−z2=x1−x2z_{1}-z_{2}=x_{1}-x_{2} and z4−z3=x1+x2z_{4}-z_{3}=x_{1}+x_{2}, and likewise for the remaining pairs, so that the six separations are exhausted by xk−xlx_{k}-x_{l} and xk+xlx_{k}+x_{l} with k<lk<l.

We expand each xkx_{k} in the circular oscillator basis |na,nb⟩\ket{n_{a}, n_{b}}, whose states carry energy na+nb+1n_{a}+n_{b}+1 and angular momentum na−nbn_{a}-n_{b}. We write mkm_{k} for the angular momentum carried by the kk-th coordinate and j=m1+m2+m3j=m_{1}+m_{2}+m_{3} for the total, which is conserved and blocks the Hamiltonian. The permutation group S4S_{4} contains the subgroup S3⋉D2S_{3}\ltimes D_{2}, where S3S_{3} permutes the xkx_{k} and D2D_{2} reverses the signs of two of them. Performing the D2D_{2} sum explicitly restricts the basis to states in which every mkm_{k} shares the parity of jj, and on that restricted sector the matrix elements of the xk+xlx_{k}+x_{l} pairs coincide with those of the xk−xlx_{k}-x_{l} pairs. The former therefore merely double the latter, and the four-anyon problem collapses onto a three-coordinate problem with doubled coupling,

H(α)=H0(x1,x2,x3)+2αW,W=−2∑k<l∂xk−∂xlx¯k−x¯l,\displaystyle H(\alpha)=H_{0}(x_{1},x_{2},x_{3})+2\alpha W\,,\qquad W=-2\sum_{k<l}\frac{\partial_{x_{k}}-\partial_{x_{l}}}{\overline{x}_{k}-\overline{x}_{l}}\,, (86)

where H0H_{0} is the oscillator Hamiltonian in the three relative coordinates. Since H0H_{0} and WW are both independent of α\alpha, and H⁡(α)H(\alpha) is exactly linear in it, each sector need only be constructed once and may then be swept over α\alpha at the cost of a single eigensolve per value.

The basis is truncated by total oscillator quanta, retaining every state for which ∑k(na,k+nb,k)⩽qmax\sum_{k}(n_{a,k}+n_{b,k})\leqslant q_{\text{max}}. Because H⁡(α)H(\alpha) is non-Hermitian we cannot use a Lanczos method. We use a generalized Davidson iteration preconditioned by the diagonal of H0H_{0}.

Convergence in qmaxq_{\text{max}} is not captured by a simple exponential or power law, and, the transformed Hamiltonian being non-Hermitian, the truncated energies are not variational. An extrapolation is therefore required, and we describe here the procedure used to produce the qmax→∞q_{\text{max}}\to\infty values of Table 1.

For α≲0.55\alpha\lesssim 0.55 the ground state is the linear branch [142] at E=4+6​αE=4+6\alpha, and at α=1\alpha=1 it is the four-fermion level E=8E=8. In both cases the exact eigenstate lies within the truncated basis and the energy is obtained to machine precision at every qmaxq_{\text{max}}, so no extrapolation is performed. For the remaining values of α\alpha the ground state lies on a different branch, and we compute a series at qmax=24,28,…,56q_{\text{max}}=24,28,\ldots,56 and fit it to

E⁡(qmax)=E0+c1​qmax−c2+c3​qmax−c4,\displaystyle E(q_{\text{max}})=E_{0}+c_{1}q_{\text{max}}^{-c_{2}}+c_{3}q_{\text{max}}^{-c_{4}}\,, (87)

with all five parameters free and the amplitudes c1c_{1} and c3c_{3} unconstrained in sign. The errors on the extrapolated energy are estimated via computing the spread of E0E_{0}’s obtained by fitting with one value of qmaxq_{\text{max}} omitted and quoting the standard deviation. The multi-exponent fit is necessary due to the non-monotonic behavior of the energy as a function of qmaxq_{\text{max}} for α=0.6\alpha=0.6. This complicated non-monotonic behavior exemplifies the difficulties in studying continuum anyonic systems with ED; although our extrapolation gives energies extremely close to our VMC results, one cannot completely rule out the possibility that other non-monotonic behavior occurs at larger qmaxq_{\text{max}} which would substantially change the prediction.

Appendix G Perturbation theory near the fermionic end

Our goal here is to evaluate ℳ\mathcal{M} in Eq. (55) analytically, so that the computation of the first-order energy correction coefficient ΛN\Lambda_{N} becomes an efficient task of computing eigenvalues of several small matrices.

G.0.1 Fermionic ground-state manifold

To facilitate the calculation of many-body matrix element ℳP​Q\mathcal{M}_{PQ}, let us adopt the following single-particle angular-momentum eigen-basis (z=x+i​yz=x+iy, z¯=x−i​y\overline{z}=x-iy):

φ𝐩​(z,z¯)=e−|z|2/2π​p+!​p−!​hp+​p−​(z,z¯),\varphi_{{\bf p}}(z,\overline{z})=\frac{e^{-\absolutevalue{z}^{2}/2}}{\sqrt{\pi p_{+}!p_{-}!}}h_{p_{+}p_{-}}(z,\overline{z}), (88)

where each orbital is labeled by 𝐩=(p+,p−)∈ℕ02{\bf p}=(p_{+},p_{-})\in\mathbb{N}_{0}^{2} (ℕ0\mathbb{N}_{0} denotes the non-negative integers), and ha​b​(z,z¯)=(−1)a+b​e|z|2​∂z¯a∂zbe−|z|2h_{ab}(z,\overline{z})=(-1)^{a+b}e^{\absolutevalue{z}^{2}}\partial^{a}_{\overline{z}}\partial^{b}_{z}e^{-\absolutevalue{z}^{2}} is known as the complex Hermite polynomial. The above orbitals constitute a complete orthonormal basis such that φ𝐩\varphi_{\bf p} has energy ε𝐩=p++p−+1\varepsilon_{\bf p}=p_{+}+p_{-}+1 (in unit of ℏ​ω\hbar\omega) and angular momentum m𝐩=p+−p−m_{\bf p}=p_{+}-p_{-} (in unit of ℏ\hbar).

The NN-fermion ground states are Slater-determinant states,

ΨP​(z1,…,zN)=1N!​det1≤a,b≤N​[φ𝐩b​(za)],\Psi_{P}(z_{1},\ldots,z_{N})=\frac{1}{\sqrt{N!}}\det_{1\leq a,b\leq N}[\varphi_{{\bf p}_{b}}(z_{a})], (89)

where here and below we suppress the z¯\overline{z} argument for simplicity. Each many-body state is specified by an ordered list of occupied orbitals: P=(𝐩1,…,𝐩N)P=({\bf p}_{1},\ldots,{\bf p}_{N}). The ordering is stipulated to be increasing in ε𝐩\varepsilon_{\bf p}, and for each fixed ε𝐩\varepsilon_{\bf p} arranged with a decreasing m𝐩m_{\bf p}. It is easy to see that the fermionic ground state energy and degeneracy, respectively, are

EN​(1)=s​(s+1)​(2​s+1)6+r⁡(s+1),DN=(s+1r),E_{N}(1)=\frac{s(s+1)(2s+1)}{6}+r(s+1),\;\;D_{N}=\binom{s+1}{r}, (90)

where the integer s⩾0s\geqslant 0 labels the highest occupied shell (with energy and degeneracy s+1s+1) which satisfies s⁡(s+1)/2<N≤(s+1)​(s+2)/2s(s+1)/2<N\leq(s+1)(s+2)/2, and r=N−s⁡(s+1)/2r=N-s(s+1)/2 is the number of fermions filling the highest shell ss. For large NN, it is clear that the fermionic ground-state energy scales as

EN​(1)∼s3/3∼N3/2​8/3.E_{N}(1)\sim s^{3}/3\sim N^{3/2}\sqrt{8}/3. (91)

Furthermore, it is useful to separate the occupied orbitals into two categories: the “core” orbitals below shell ss and the “valence” orbitals in shell ss. Figure 12 shows an illustration for organizing the fermionic ground states.

G.0.2 Many-body matrix elements

Combining Eq. (55) with Eq. (89), we obtain a compact form for the many-body matrix elements in terms of two-body matrix elements:

ℳP​Q=∑i<j,k<lPi​j=Qk​l(−1)i+j+k+l​W𝐩i​𝐩j,𝐪k​𝐪l,\mathcal{M}_{PQ}=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}i<j,\ k<l\\ P_{ij}=Q_{kl}\end{subarray}}(-1)^{i+j+k+l}W_{{\bf p}_{i}{\bf p}_{j},{\bf q}_{k}{\bf q}_{l}}, (92)

where Pi​jP_{ij} corresponds to the list of occupied orbitals with 𝐩i{\bf p}_{i} and 𝐩j{\bf p}_{j} removed, and

W𝐩𝐪,𝐫𝐬\displaystyle W_{{\bf p}{\bf q},{\bf r}{\bf s}} =⟨σ𝐩𝐪|​V^12​|σ𝐫𝐬⟩,\displaystyle=\bra{\sigma_{\bp\bq}}\widehat{V}_{12}\ket{\sigma_{\br\bs}}, (93a)
σ𝐩𝐪​(z1,z2)\displaystyle\sigma_{{\bf p}{\bf q}}(z_{1},z_{2}) =12​[φ𝐩​(z1)​φ𝐪​(z2)−φ𝐪​(z1)​φ𝐩​(z2)].\displaystyle=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\varphi_{{\bf p}}(z_{1})\varphi_{{\bf q}}(z_{2})-\varphi_{{\bf q}}(z_{1})\varphi_{{\bf p}}(z_{2})]. (93b)

Energy and angular momentum constraints dictate that the two-body matrix elements W𝐩𝐪,𝐫𝐬W_{{\bf p}{\bf q},{\bf r}{\bf s}} of concern must obey p++q+=r++s+p_{+}+q_{+}=r_{+}+s_{+} and p−+q−=r−+s−p_{-}+q_{-}=r_{-}+s_{-}. The two-body integral in W𝐩𝐪,𝐫𝐬W_{{\bf p}{\bf q},{\bf r}{\bf s}} can be carried out analytically, resulting in

W𝐩𝐪,𝐫𝐬=2​∑0≤i≤p, 0≤j≤qi+j​oddsgn⁡(i−j)​Ci​j𝐩𝐪​Ci​j𝐫𝐬,W_{{\bf p}{\bf q},{\bf r}{\bf s}}=2\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}0\leq i\leq p,\ 0\leq j\leq q\\ i+j\ \mathrm{odd}\end{subarray}}\operatorname{sgn}(i-j)\,C_{ij}^{{\bf p}{\bf q}}C_{ij}^{{\bf r}{\bf s}}, (94)

where we have defined p≡p++q+p\equiv p_{+}+q_{+}, q≡p−+q−q\equiv p_{-}+q_{-}, and

Ci​j𝐩𝐪\displaystyle C_{ij}^{{\bf p}{\bf q}} =(p−i)!​(q−j)!​i!​j!2p+q​p+!​p−!​q+!​q−!​Bip+,q+​Bjp−,q−,\displaystyle=\sqrt{\frac{(p-i)!(q-j)!i!j!}{2^{p+q}\;p_{+}!p_{-}!q_{+}!q_{-}!}}B_{i}^{p_{+},q_{+}}B_{j}^{p_{-},q_{-}}, (95a)
Bia,b\displaystyle B_{i}^{a,b} =∑k=0i(−1)i−k​(ak)​(bi−k).\displaystyle=\sum_{k=0}^{i}(-1)^{i-k}\binom{a}{k}\binom{b}{i-k}. (95b)

To shed some light on Eq. (94), let us mention that Ci​j𝐩𝐪C_{ij}^{{\bf p}{\bf q}} is a combinatorial factor serving as an expansion coefficient for the two-fermion state σ𝐩𝐪​(z1,z2)\sigma_{{\bf p}{\bf q}}(z_{1},z_{2}) in terms of the center-of-mass Z=(z1+z2)/2Z=(z_{1}+z_{2})/\sqrt{2} and relative u=(z1−z2)/2u=(z_{1}-z_{2})/\sqrt{2} coordinates:

σ𝐩𝐪=2​∑0≤i≤p, 0≤j≤qi+j​oddCi​j𝐩𝐪​φp−i,q−j​(Z)​φi​j​(u).\sigma_{{\bf p}{\bf q}}=\sqrt{2}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}0\leq i\leq p,\ 0\leq j\leq q\\ i+j\ \mathrm{odd}\end{subarray}}C_{ij}^{{\bf p}{\bf q}}\,\varphi_{p-i,q-j}(Z)\varphi_{ij}(u). (96)

Only odd i+ji+j contribute due to the fermionic antisymmetry and the fact that φi​j​(−u)=(−1)i+j​φi​j​(u)\varphi_{ij}(-u)=(-1)^{i+j}\varphi_{ij}(u), while the factor sgn⁡(i−j)\operatorname{sgn}(i-j) in Eq. (94) is the result of the relative-coordinate integral.

G.0.3 ΛN\Lambda_{N} as a benchmark

Combining Eqs. (54), (92), (94) and  (95), we have all the ingredients needed to compute ΛN\Lambda_{N}. Notice that the summation in Eq. (92) can be largely reduced by discarding terms where both 𝐩i{\bf p}_{i} and 𝐩j{\bf p}_{j} (accordingly, 𝐪k{\bf q}_{k} and 𝐪l{\bf q}_{l}) are core orbitals, as the sum over all these terms must vanish by the fact that V^12\widehat{V}_{12} is odd under time-reversal.

As an explicit example, take N=4N=4, where we have three degenerate fermionic ground states that share the same core orbitals: 𝐩1=(0,0){\bf p}_{1}=(0,0), 𝐩2=(1,0){\bf p}_{2}=(1,0) and 𝐩3=(0,1){\bf p}_{3}=(0,1), and distinguished by their single valence orbital: 𝐩4=(2,0),(1,1),(0,2){\bf p}_{4}=(2,0),\;(1,1),\;(0,2), which give them distinct total angular momenta (and hence ℳ\mathcal{M} is diagonal as constructed). The relevant terms in Eq. (92) are W𝐩i​𝐩4,𝐩i​𝐩4W_{{\bf p}_{i}{\bf p}_{4},{\bf p}_{i}{\bf p}_{4}} (i=1,2,3i=1,2,3), which are tabulated in Table 4. From this we obtain Λ4=5/2\Lambda_{4}=5/2, consistent with the result obtained earlier using the non-relativistic conformal field theory technique [92].

With the method developed above, we can systematically obtain ΛN\Lambda_{N} for a range of NN. In Table 2, for a selected set of NN we have documented a comparison between the exact perturbation theory results with our quadratic fitting results obtained from the anyonic NNVMC simulations with α=0.98,0.99,0.995,0.9975\alpha=0.98,0.99,0.995,0.9975 and 11. The observed close numerical match, which is also shown in Fig. 6, demonstrates the effectiveness of our AnyNet ansatze for simulating intermediate scale anyonic systems. We further observe from Fig. 6 that ΛN\Lambda_{N} scales as N3/2N^{3/2} at large NN, similar to the fermionic ground state energy EN​(1)E_{N}(1) in Eq. (91). This is a direct demonstration of an effective attraction (or a weakened Pauli exclusion) in an almost-fermionic anyon gas.
